name: Philip Morris

summary.text: Philip Morris is a cigarette manufacturer whose U.S. business, Philip Morris USA, is a subsidiary of Altria Group; Altria spun off Philip Morris International to its shareholders on March 28, 2008. Philip Morris was one of four major tobacco companies that signed the 1998 Master Settlement Agreement with 46 state attorneys general, committing the industry to about $206 billion in payments over 25 years. In August 2006, after a nine-month bench trial in United States v. Philip Morris, Judge Gladys Kessler found the company and other defendants liable under the civil RICO statute for a decades-long conspiracy to deceive the public about the health effects of smoking and ordered corrective statements. In 1993 the firm Burson-Marsteller created the National Smokers Alliance on Philip Morris's behalf.

facts.claim: On August 17, 2006, after a nine-month bench trial, Judge Gladys Kessler of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia found that the defendants in United States v. Philip Morris had violated RICO through a lengthy, unlawful conspiracy to deceive the American public about the health effects of smoking and environmental tobacco smoke, the addictiveness of nicotine, the health benefits of low-tar and "light" cigarettes, and their manipulation of cigarette design; the opinion ran about 1,683 pages.
facts.quote: a lengthy, unlawful conspiracy to deceive the American public about the health effects of smoking and environmental tobacco smoke, the addictiveness of nicotine, the health benefits from low tar, 'light' cigarettes, and their manipulation of the design and composition of cigarettes.

sources.title: United States v. Philip Morris USA

facts.claim: Because the D.C. Circuit had read RICO as allowing only forward-looking remedies, the court did not order the companies to fund smoking cessation or public education programs, but it required corrective statements on five subjects (addiction, health effects of smoking and secondhand smoke, nicotine manipulation, and "light" and "low tar" cigarettes) and found a reasonable likelihood of future violations as long as the defendants remained in the business of selling and marketing tobacco products.
facts.quote: as long as Defendants [we]re in the business of selling and marketing tobacco products," there was a "reasonable likelihood" that they would violate RICO again.

sources.title: Everything You Ever Wanted to Know about U.S. v. Philip Morris

facts.claim: On appeal, the D.C. Circuit in 2009 directed that corrective statements be confined to purely factual and uncontroversial information and vacated the point-of-sale display requirement; in 2015 it upheld most of the implementing order but rejected a preamble stating that a federal court had ruled the companies "deliberately deceived the American public"; in 2017 it deleted the phrase "Here is the truth."
facts.quote: the court rejected a preamble sentence that a federal court had ruled the tobacco companies "deliberately deceived the American public," ruling it was not permissible under the scope of the RICO law.

facts.claim: Altria's board announced on January 30, 2008 a plan to spin off Philip Morris International to Altria stockholders in a tax-free transaction under Section 355 of the Internal Revenue Code; on March 28, 2008 Altria distributed one PMI share for each Altria share, after which Altria owned no PMI stock and retained the U.S. business.
facts.quote: Altria distributed one share of PMI common stock for each share of Altria common stock outstanding as of the Record Date.
